title.en: Kêng Sang Ch'u Refuses to Be a Tutelary God (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 庚桑楚居畏壘之山（莊子）

region.en: The Wei-lei mountains in the north (symbolic pin: Yimengshan, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 畏壘之山（象徵定位：山東沂蒙山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 23, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 23

summary.en: Kêng Sang Ch'u, the only disciple of Lao Tzŭ to attain his TAO, lives on the Wei-lei mountains, dismissing clever and charitable attendants — and in three years the district is greatly benefited. The villagers ask to honour him as a tutelary god; he turns his face south in shame, and prophesies that a thousand ages hence man will be feeding upon man.
summary.zh: 老聃之役有庚桑楚者，偏得老聃之道，北居畏壘之山；居三年，畏壘大壤。相與言曰：庶幾其聖人乎——胡為乎尸祝而社稷之乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); Keng-sang became a canonized immortal of the Zhuangzi's first 'outer' chapter. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Among the disciples of Lao Tzŭ was one named Kêng Sang Ch'u. He alone had attained to the TAO of his Master. He lived up north, on the Wei-lei Mountains. Of his attendants, he dismissed those who were systematically clever or conventionally charitable. The useless remained with him; the incompetent served him. And in three years the district of Wei-lei was greatly benefited.

One of the inhabitants said in conversation, "When Mr. Kêng Sang first came among us, we did not know what to make of him. Now, we could not say enough about him in a day, and even a year would leave something unsaid. Surely he must be a true Sage. Why not pray to him as to the spirits, and honour him as a tutelary god of the land?" On hearing of this, Kêng Sang Ch'u turned his face to the south in shame, at which his disciples were astonished. But Kêng Sang said, "What cause have you for astonishment? The influence of spring quickens the life of plants, and autumn brings them to maturity. In the absence of any agent, how is this so? It is the operation of TAO.

"A beast big enough to swallow a cart, if it wanders alone from the hills, will not escape the sorrow of the snare. A fish big enough to gulp down a boat, if stranded on the dry shore will become a prey to ants. Therefore it is that birds and beasts love height, and fishes and turtles love depth. And the man who cares for himself hides his body. He loves the occult. ... If the virtuous are honoured, emulation will ensue. If knowledge be fostered, the result will be theft. ... I tell you that the root of this great evil is from Yao and Shun, and that its branches will extend into a thousand ages to come. A thousand ages hence, man will be feeding upon man!"

title.en: Nan Yung Ch'u's Seven Days' Journey to Lao Tzŭ (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's abode (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老子之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 23, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 23

summary.en: Nan Yung Ch'u carries provisions on a seven days' journey to Lao Tzŭ with three dilemmas: if I do not know, men call me a fool; if I do know, I injure myself; and charity injures both others and myself. The sage teaches the art of preserving life — to be as a child, crying all day without becoming hoarse — and warns that there is no weapon so deadly as man's will.
summary.zh: 南榮趎贏糧，七日七夜至老子之所。老子曰：衛生之經——能抱一乎？能勿失乎？一純素之道，惟神是守。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the classic teaching-scene of the 'art of preserving life'. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: So Nan Yung took some provisions, and after a seven days' journey arrived at the abode of Lao Tzŭ. "Have you come from Kêng Sang Ch'u?" said the latter. "I have," replied Nan Yung. "But why," said Lao Tzŭ, "bring all these people with you?" Nan Yung looked back in alarm, and Lao Tzŭ continued, "Do you not understand what I say?" Nan Yung bent his head abashed, and then looking up, said with a sigh, "I have now forgotten how to answer, in consequence of missing what I came to ask."

If I do not know," replied Nan Yung, "men call me a fool. If I do know, I injure myself. If I am not charitable, I injure others. If I am, I injure myself. If I do not do my duty to my neighbour, I injure others. If I do it, I injure myself. My trouble lies in not seeing how to escape from these three dilemmas.

"The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, to lose nothing, to estimate good and evil without divination, to know when to stop, and how much is enough, to leave others alone and attend to oneself, to be without cares and without knowledge,--to be in fact as a child. A child will cry all day and not become hoarse, because of the perfection of its constitutional harmony. ... "There is no weapon so deadly as man's will. Excalibur is second to it. There is no bandit so powerful as Nature. In the whole universe there is no escape from it. Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart."
